name: Hand drying footprint

summary: The Hand drying footprint calculator turns the towels used, number of staff and the time per dry into hand drying frequency. It is built for a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Hand drying footprint calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hand drying footprint calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports hand drying frequency in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the use and the hand drying system); then you type in the towels used, number of staff, the towels used (staff) and the time per dry (staff).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hand drying footprint calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

How many times are you washing your hands?=carbon footprint ÷ (towels used × hand drying system)
Hand drying frequency (staff)=(-hand drying frequency (customers) × customers × towels used (customers) + total towels per day) ÷ (towels used (staff) × number of staff)
Total towels per day=total towels per year ÷ workdays in a year
Total towels per year=carbon footprint ÷ hand drying system
Trees saved (from logging for paper towels)=(1 ÷ 25000) × total towels per year
Trees cut for paper production=(1 ÷ 25000) × total towels per year

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Use set to Office / public spaces, Hand drying system set to Paper towels (recycled), Towels used = 2 and Times per dry = 0.0086 sec. Straight away the calculator returns Carbon footprint = 7.4 g and Trees needed to absorb it = 7.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Carbon footprint = 7.4 g and Trees needed to absorb it = 7 should be roughly the size you expected from Use set to Office / public spaces and Hand drying system set to Paper towels (recycled).

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hand drying footprint calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the towels used, number of staff and the time per dry — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hand drying footprint calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns hand drying frequency, derived from the towels used, number of staff and the time per dry. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hand drying footprint calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the towels used, number of staff and the time per dry, which is 25 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter times per dry in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Times per dry opens in seconds and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Carbon footprint = 7.4 g. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hand drying footprint calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
